overview.description: Leyden is a two-player domino game named after the university city in South Holland. It is a variant of the 'Matador' family of domino games, characterized by the 'Rule of Seven'â€”players must build arms from a central spinner by matching adjacent ends so they total exactly seven. The game features special 'Matador' tiles that can be played on any end regardless of the sum rule.

history.origins: Believed to have developed in the 19th century as a variant of the Matador domino family. The name 'Leyden' (Leiden in Dutch) refers to the university city in South Holland, though the exact historical connection is unclear.
timeline: 1880s: Matador-style connecting games spread through Northern Europe.
1920s: Leyden rules are codified in Dutch gaming manuals.
Present: Primarily played as a competitive logic game for two players, valued for its mathematical simplicity and strategic depth.
history.evolution: The game was traditionally played with wooden tiles but adapted into card formats for easier transport during the early 20th century. The rules have remained relatively stable, with only minor regional variations.
history.cultural: Used in educational settings to teach basic arithmetic and strategic blocking. Popular among students, which may explain the university city name association.

setup.deck: Standard double-six domino set (28 tiles:  through ).
setup.dealing: Each player draws 6 tiles. The remaining 16 tiles form the boneyard (stock), placed face-down.

rules.objective: Be the first player to reach 100 points. Points are scored based on the total pips remaining in your opponent's hand when a round ends (or when you domino).
rules.gameplay: 1. : The player with the lowest double (excluding ) leads that double to start the first round. After the first round, the loser of the previous round leads and must lead a double other than . 2. : The first double played is the spinner for the round. The first four plays must be on the four sides of the spinner, starting all four arms of the cross before any arm can be extended further. 3. : To place a regular tile, the end of the arm where it is played and the adjacent end of the played tile must total exactly 7. Valid pairs are: 1-6, 2-5, and 3-4. 4. : The four special tiles , , , and  can be played on any end without regard to the Rule of Seven. 5. : A player can choose to draw as many tiles as desired on their turn, but must leave at least 2 tiles in the boneyard. A player with no play must continue drawing until they find a playable tile or the boneyard is reduced to 2 tiles.
keyRules: Lowest double (not ) leads the first round.
First double is the spinner; four arms must be started before extending.
Rule of Seven: adjacent ends must total exactly 7 (1-6, 2-5, 3-4).
Matadors , , ,  can play on any end.
Arm ending in 0 can only be extended by a Matador.
Must leave at least 2 tiles in boneyard when drawing.
First to 100 points loses (standard) or wins (variant).

strategy.basic: Keep your Matadors! Since they can clear any blocked arm, they are your only way to save a round when the table is filled with cards that have no 'Seven' matches left. Don't waste them early.
strategy.intermediate: Suit Control: Try to hold two strong suits that total to seven, such as the 2s and the 5s. This gives you flexibility in playing regular tiles. Watch the blanksâ€”once an arm ends in 0, only a Matador can extend it.
strategy.advanced: The Zero Strategy: The 0-0 Matador is the most dangerous tile. If you play it across an arm, the next player MUST play another Matador to continue it. Use this to force your opponent to use their best tiles prematurely. Offensive Drawing: If you have a clear lead, don't be afraid to draw from the boneyard even if you have a play, as long as the boneyard is large. This 'starves' the opponent of Matadors hidden in the stock.
tips: Always check the count of '4s' and '3s' on the board. Since they match each other, a shortage of one rank makes the other rank unplayable.
If you are the starting player, lead with a double-3 or double-4 to create immediate branching paths.
Don't go crazy drawing tiles. Getting stuck with a big hand will cost you points if your opponent dominoes.
The  Matador is the most flexibleâ€”save it for emergencies.

difficulty.easy: Fails to recognize Matadors; misses 'Seven' matches; draws too many tiles early; doesn't block arms strategically.
difficulty.medium: Conserves Matadors for late-game blocks; understands basic sum-seven distribution; recognizes when to force opponent to use Matadors.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'Boneyard Starvation'; perfectly tracks the 28-tile rank count; masters the [0-0] block strategy; optimal arm extension planning; anticipates opponent's tile holdings.

customActions.description: Determine which player holds the lowest double (excluding [0-0]); that player leads the first round. In later rounds the previous round loser leads and must lead a double other than [0-0].
customActions.constraints: Dealer or system; before play phase.

customActions.description: Place a tile on an arm of the cross. Regular tiles: the arm end and the adjacent end of the played tile must total seven (1-6, 2-5, 3-4). Matadors [1-6], [2-5], [3-4], [0-0] may be played on any end. First double is the spinner; first four plays start the four arms.
customActions.constraints: Current player; tile must match Rule of Seven or be a Matador; doubles played in line.

customActions.description: Draw one or more tiles from the boneyard (stock). Player may draw as many as desired but must leave at least two tiles in the boneyard. A player with no legal play must draw until they have a playable tile or the boneyard is reduced to two tiles.
customActions.constraints: On your turn; at least two tiles must remain in the boneyard; neither player may draw when only two remain.

customActions.description: Round ends when a player plays their last tile (dominoes). That player wins the round.
customActions.constraints: System outcome when current player's hand is empty after a play.

customActions.description: Round ends in a block when no player can play and the boneyard has two or fewer tiles. Winner is the player with fewer pips in hand; if equal, no score and same player leads next round.
customActions.constraints: System outcome when no legal play exists and boneyard is depleted to two tiles.

customActions.description: Round continues; play passes to the next player.
customActions.constraints: System outcome when round has not ended by domino or block.

customActions.description: Score the round: winner receives the total pips in opponent's hand (or both hands in blocked equal-points case per variant). First to 100 points loses; if both over 100 in same round, lowest score wins.

engine.handRankingSystem: Points based on pips in opponent's hand when round ends; no card hand ranking.
engine.deckDescription: Double-six domino set of 28 tiles: each tile has two ends with pip values from 0 to 6, from [0-0] through [6-6]. No suits; tiles are identified by their two end values. Used for Matador-style connecting games where adjacent ends must total seven.
engine.suitDescription: Dominoes do not use suits; each tile has two ends with values 0-6. The set is the standard double-six layout of 28 unique tiles.
engine.rankDescription: Each end of a domino has a pip value from 0 (blank) to 6. Tiles are named by their two ends, e.g. [3-4] or [0-0]. The four Matadors [1-6], [2-5], [3-4], [0-0] total seven or zero and act as wilds.
engine.dealPattern: Six tiles to each player; the remaining sixteen tiles form the boneyard (stock), face down.

synthesis.shortDescription: A two-player domino game where tiles must be played so adjacent ends sum to seven, with special Matador tiles that break the rules.

prompts.human: Welcome to Leyden! Build arms from the central spinner by making adjacent ends sum to seven. Your 2 matches their 5, your 3 matches their 4. Use Matador tiles ([1-6], [2-5], [3-4], [0-0]) to break the rules when you're stuck. First to 100 points losesâ€”empty your hand to score!
prompts.ai: Game: Leyden. 2 players, double-six dominoes (28 tiles). Deal 6 each, 16 to boneyard. Lowest double leads. First double is spinner (4 arms). Rule of Seven: adjacent ends must total 7 (1-6, 2-5, 3-4). Matadors [1-6],[2-5],[3-4],[0-0] can play anywhere. [0-0] blocks arms. Score opponent's pips when you domino. First to 100 loses.
